title: Ingress spreadbench (autocorrelated load) - notes
body:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad for a new ingress spreadbench that injects autocorrelated inter-arrival times (to mimic client-side batching/clustering) rather than pure Poisson. Goal is to observe queueing tails and KV-cache effectiveness when short bursts cluster on top of baseline QPS.

High-level idea:
- Replace exponential inter-arrivals with an AR(1)-style correlated generator (rho ~ 0.6) so requests come in patches separated by quieter intervals.
- Sweep baseline qps (10, 50, 200) and overlay burst magnitude factors (1.5x, 3x, 6x) and burst length distributions (short: 10-50ms, medium: 50-200ms, long: 200-800ms).
- Run against a single-serving-node dedicated instance (A100xlarge prod-like) with model redwood-small-v1 (quantized fp16).

Setup specifics:
- Harness: local runner -> gateway -> serving node. Synthetic client uses golang harness (randseed fixed) with adjustable autocorr param.
- Model: redwood-small-v1, seq_len=512, batchable op, kv-cache enabled.
- Concurrency target: single request per connection; use 1000 client goroutines for high baseline qps regimes.
- Duration: 5 min per sweep point (after 1m warmup).
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (server-side and client-side), qps observed, queue depth histogram, KV cache hit rate (prefix share), GPU utilization, scheduling stalls (runtime logs).

Key run matrix (abridged):
- Baselines: 10 qps, 50 qps, 200 qps
- Burst factors: 1.5, 3.0, 6.0
- Burst durations: short/med/long as above
- Autocorr rho: 0.0 (control), 0.3, 0.6

Representative raw observations (selected cases):
1) Baseline 50 qps, burst x3, medium duration, rho=0.6:
- client p50/p95/p99: 24ms / 120ms / 420ms
- server p50/p95/p99 (token-output measured): 18ms / 92ms / 380ms
- peak queue depth: 42 (observed 30–60 depending on burst timing)
- kv-cache hit rate: 68% (dropped to ~55% during long bursts)
- GPU util: 73% nominal -> spikes to 94% during bursts
- notes: tail dominated by queueing; single long burst aligned with a cache-miss window amplified p99

2) Baseline 200 qps, burst x1.5, short duration, rho=0.6:
- client p50/p95/p99: 12ms / 42ms / 120ms
- server p50/p95/p99: 10ms / 36ms / 95ms
- peak queue depth: 18
- kv-cache hit rate: 82%
- gpu util: 88% steady -> short spikes 98%
- notes: system handles mild clustered bursts well; tails modest, kv-cache absorbs prefix overlap nicely

3) Baseline 10 qps, burst x6, long duration, rho=0.6:
- client p50/p95/p99: 34ms / 520ms / 1800ms
- server p50/p95/p99: 30ms / 460ms / 1600ms
- peak queue depth: 180+ (queueing hit limits, started backpressure)
- kv-cache hit rate: 12% (cache cold during extended burst of unique contexts)
- gpu util: 35% -> sudden ramp to 100% causing scheduler preemption events
- notes: worst-case; burst injects too many concurrent origin-like requests with low prefix reuse causing cache churn and long p99s

Quick ascii timeline (50 qps, burst x3 medium, rho=0.6):

time(ms)  |  0  50 100 150 200 250 300 350 400 450 500
requests  |  8  12 18 40 35 25 18 14 10 8 6
queue     |  2  6  10 26 30 24 12 6 3 2 1
latency p99(ms) | 40 55 90 380 320 200 120 70 45 40 38

Immediate takeaways (rough):
- Autocorrelation matters: rho>0.5 creates sustained patches that overwhelm batching heuristics tuned for memoryless arrivals.
- KV-cache effectiveness declines when burst arrival contains many unique prompts; but moderate clustering with repeat prefixes improves hit-rate and smooths tails.
- Backpressure/backoff config currently steps in too late for long high-magnitude bursts; need earlier shedding tiers or soft-degradation path (serve cached-only responses / shorter generation length)
- Scheduler preemption observed when GPU utilization spikes abruptly — this correlates with OS-level scheduling events (investigate CUDA stream preemption, MPS config).

Open questions / next experiments:
- How do canary-level autoscaling policies perform when ingress exhibits high autocorr? Run same harness against 2-node pool (same model) with redwood routing to test redispatch/fanout impact.
- Can dynamic batching window adapt to recent autocorr signal and temporarily shrink windows to reduce queueing? Add adaptive batch timeout probe.
- Investigate tiny-model vs medium-model behavior: are tails worse on larger models due to longer service time variability? Run opt-1.3b and redwood-medium-v1.
- Try synthetic bursts that keep prefix overlap constant vs fully random to isolate KV cache effect.

Action items (short):
- [ ] Add an 'autocorr' flag to our standard ingress load generator and submit to common harness (PR linked above).
- [ ] Run 2-node fanout comparison (priority) — follow-up by 2026-03-17. Assigned: Lina.
- [ ] Add probe that records CUDA stream preemption logs + kernel timestamps (ask infra).
- [ ] Draft short runbook: early-shedding thresholds and when to flip to cached-only responses (writeup for prod runbook).

Notes-to-self / friction:
- Harness currently logs client-side times only; need synchronized server-side tracing to attribute tail to queue vs compute.
- Random seed matters: keep seed fixed to make runs reproducible for debug, but also run few randomized seeds to sanity-check variance.
- Some runs produced outlier p99s that correlated with background cron snapshot job on host — pin host to maintenance-exempt for clean runs.

References / context:
- Related ticket INF-5567: ingress overload protection roadmap.
- PR: fixing adaptive batch timeout heuristic: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1189

Bottom-line (working hypothesis):
Ingress autocorrelation (client clustering) is a realistic shape that amplifies p99s mainly via queueing and cache churn. Mitigations likely need a combo of early shedding, adaptive batching, and routing/fanout strategies rather than single knob tuning.

End of scratchpad.

-- Priyanka (notes)
